book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles

chapters.file: ch03 - The Blackwell Philosophy and Pop Culture Series.md

chapters.relation: Tom Morris recounts how the 2004 volume Harry Potter and Philosophy: If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts showed that academics were finding real wisdom in Rowling's series, and how he went from skeptic to reading all seven books six times and writing his own book on their insights into courage, love, and death. He presents this new collection, written after the series ended, as a 'Philosophical De-coder Ring' that reveals the deepest story behind the novels.

The introduction argues, citing Plato's saying that philosophy begins in wonder, that children's fantasy like Rowling's is a natural home for philosophy, since young readers can be nourished by ideas they cannot fully digest, like Fang gnawing a dragon bone. It canvasses the volume's guiding questions: whether love is the most powerful magic, whether souls exist and can be split by Horcruxes, what Animagi and boggarts teach about personal identity, whether choices reveal more than abilities, and whether Snape can be redeemed. It closes by framing the book in the Blackwell series tradition of using pop culture to teach philosophy, updating the 2004 Open Court volume now that all seven novels are out.

chapters.file: ch10 - PART ONE - THE HORCRUX OF THE MATTER DESTINY, IDENTITY, AND THE SOUL.md
ch11 - Philosophical Conceptions of the Soul.md

chapters.relation: This section of the soul chapter lays out the Cartesian view: the immaterial soul explains only language and higher-level cognition, while material causes suffice for sensation, which consigns nonhuman animals to soullessness. It applies the view to Rowling's borderline creatures, such as owls that understand human speech and Crookshanks's suspicious intelligence, before introducing materialism as the fourth conception of the soul.

The section argues that everyday talk of soul mates, soulful art, and baring one's soul is metaphorical talk about our deepest emotions, love, and conscience, not commitment to an immaterial substance, and that even materialists can keep the vocabulary rather than translate Hoagy Carmichael into talk of C-fibers firing. It then forecasts the chapter's conclusion about Rowling: her Potter-world soul mixes this sentimental view with metaphysics borrowed from the Cartesian and sentience views.

The section argues that materialism is false in the Potter universe by cataloguing the ways souls outlive bodies: Hermione's claim that a sword through Ron would leave his soul untouched, the voices beyond the Ministry's veil, Nearly Headless Nick's ghostly imprint of a wizard who refused to 'go on,' Voldemort's wraith-like survival, and the 'neither ghost nor truly flesh' shades summoned from Voldemort's wand and by the Resurrection Stone. It sets up dementors and Horcruxes as the next tests of what souls are.

Using Lupin's account of the Dementor's Kiss, in which the victim goes on existing as an empty shell with no sense of self or memory, the section rules out the life-source and sentience views of the soul and probably the Cartesian view too, since a soulless Barty Crouch Jr. might still perceive the room. The author proposes the soulless state is like severe dementia or Lockhart after his backfired memory charm, raising the question of what, if anything, makes the shell still a person.

Reconstructing Slughorn's lesson to young Riddle, the section argues that because Voldemort's brain, senses, and magical powers survive his soul being ripped into seven, the Cartesian and sentience views are excluded and Rowling must hold the sentimental view: the soul is our capacity to love and our moral conscience. Voldemort's snake-faced transformation and his followers' fear-based loyalty, where even Bellatrix worships his power rather than being charmed, dramatize his lost humanity, and only remorse, which Harry begs him to 'try for' before the rebounding curse kills him, could have repaired the damage.

The concluding section of the soul essay asks whether Rowling's combined theory is likely true and answers probably not: there is no evidence of immaterial causes of brain events, the centuries-old mind-body interaction problem looms, and it is especially implausible that a separate substance handles only our deepest emotions and moral traits, with the added wrinkle that souls in the story display different physical powers depending on which spell conjures them. Yet it concedes that implausible metaphysics is no flaw in fiction that makes vivid what we care about and 'makes for a terrific story.'

Opening Eric Saidel's chapter, the section takes Sirius's tail-chasing as Padfoot in Order of the Phoenix as its puzzle: is Sirius a man sometimes in a dog's body, a dog sometimes in a man's body, or a third 'someone' who persists through the change? It widens the question to Pettigrew, Rita Skeeter, McGonagall, werewolf Lupin, boggarts, and Polyjuice transformations, framing it as a question about identity and the mind-body relation.

The section applies the Cartesian division of persons into mind plus body, generating four possible descriptions of Padfoot such as Sirius's mind in a dog's body, and shows each fails: McGonagall's 'non-being' quip cannot house Sirius's vanished body, and neither pairing explains why Padfoot both chases his tail and stands on his hind legs to see Harry off at King's Cross. So the mind-body distinction cannot say what the transformed Sirius is.

chapters.file: ch25 - A Step in the Right Direction.md
chapters.relation: Recasting the puzzle as a question of whose reasons cause Padfoot's actions, the section shows that strategy fails too: Harry as Runcorn and Ron as Cattermole act on Harry's and Ron's own reasons, never on those of the men whose bodies they wear, and dogs chase tails because it feels good, not for reasons at all. So reasons cannot explain either Padfoot's tail-chasing or werewolf Lupin's attacks, which come from his blood while his reasons would restrain him.

The section tries a division of labor in which Sirius's mind explains his human gestures while his dog's body explains the tail-chasing, tested by the thought experiment of Sirius having become a bear instead, who would have done bear things rather than chase a tail he never had. But the price is absurdity: pleasure must reside in the body, giving Padfoot's body reasons of its own that could clash with Sirius's mind, as in 'I didn't want to chase my tail, but my body wanted to,' so the mind/body split buckles.

The section rejects the 'captain of a ship' picture of mind directing body, quoting Descartes himself on being so 'compounded and intermingled' with the body as to form 'a single whole,' and reads the Polyjuice episodes as proof: Harry in Runcorn's body naturally 'thunders' with a powerful voice and punches with an enormous fist, while Luna recognizes Harry through 'Barny's' face, impossible if mind and body were separable. The conclusion is that transformed people are unified man-dog wholes, and that even Muggle changes such as weight loss, learning to ride a bike, or Crouch-as-Moody show that changing our bodies changes who we are.

The section sets up Jeremy Pierce's chapter by contrasting Trelawney the 'old fraud,' whose tea leaves, tarot, and crystal balls yield elastic generalities and false death forecasts, with the two predictions Dumbledore calls her only 'real predictions,' which McGonagall and the centaur Firenze also treat as different in kind. It asks what distinguishes genuine prophecy from fortune-telling in a world where magic might connect tea leaves or dreams to actual future events.

Crediting Aristotle with first raising whether the future is fixed, the section distinguishes fallible from infallible prophecies and builds a seven-fold menu of how a Seer could access the future, from fallible sense-based guessing like Muggle weather reports and Trelawney's usual act, through probabilities over possible futures, to infallible access to a deterministic outcome or to the actual fixed future. The question becomes which of these Trelawney's two genuine prophecies are.

The section argues that Dumbledore treats even the real prophecy as fallible, telling Harry he is 'quite free to turn your back on the prophecy,' which suggests likelihood rather than guarantee. Yet the involuntary trance source, Trelawney's spade readings that fit the hidden Harry she cannot see, and the lightning-struck tower card point to occasional access to possible or fixed futures beyond mere category-1 guessing.

Testing whether Trelawney's first prophecy was self-fulfilling, the section deploys Alexander of Aphrodisias's discussion of the Oedipus story, where a prediction that causes its own fulfillment would be the prophet's deed rather than a revelation of what was going to happen. It concludes the prophecy did not make Voldemort attack: he chose Harry as the half-blood he saw himself in, acting on incomplete information from Snape's interrupted eavesdropping, so self-fulfillment cannot distinguish real predictions from Trelawney's usual fare.

The section spells out what Rowling's reported denial of destiny could mean, laying out compatibilism versus libertarian freedom and fixed versus open futures on which statements about future free choices lack truth values. Dumbledore's insistence that Harry could have turned his back on the prophecy fits either a genuinely open future or a fixed one that prophecies do not compel, so the books themselves must decide.

chapters.file: ch34 - Time Travel and Fixed Time.md
chapters.relation: The section argues the second real prophecy, about the servant rejoining the Dark Lord that night, cannot be merely 'likely but fallible': Wormtail's escape depended on a chain of improbable contingencies such as Lupin forgetting his Wolfsbane potion and the last-minute switch of Secret-Keeper. The first prophecy likewise required Voldemort to mark Harry through events, from Snape's plea to Lily's sacrifice, that flow from the prophecy itself, so genuine prophecy needs a stronger tie to the actual future than probability.

The section defends fixed time from the Prisoner of Azkaban episode, where later-Harry casts the stag Patronus that saved earlier-Harry and nothing about the past changes, against Hermione's warnings that wizards have killed their past selves, which the author recasts as travel between possible timelines. A special-relativity argument that there is no absolute present supports fixed time, and the cascade of lucky coincidences from brewing Polyjuice in Moaning Myrtle's bathroom through Felix Felicis, Malfoy Manor, and the Shrieking Shack finally suggests that some providential guide, rather than dumb luck, steered events toward the prophecy's fulfillment.

chapters.file: ch37 - PART TWO - THE MOST POWERFUL MAGIC OF ALL.md
ch38 - Snape and the Many-Splendored Thing.md
chapters.relation: The section opens the Deavels' chapter with the puzzle of Dumbledore's 'ironclad reason' for trusting Snape even after Snape kills him, recalling McGonagall's 'he trusted... always,' and names the answer: Snape's unrequited love for Lily, which leads circuitously to his redemption. It previews the philosophical questions about the nature and varieties of love and its power to blind judgment that the chapter will bring to Snape's story.

Surveying eros, philia, and agape, from the Weasleys' romantic love to Voldemort's never having wanted a friend to 'God is love,' the section draws on Plato's Symposium, where crude physical desire is progressively refined toward the beautiful and divine, to argue that love is primarily a choice of the will rather than a feeling. Hence Snape's continuing dislike of Harry is no evidence against his transformation by love; acting for others' good despite his emotions is precisely the testimony to it.

The section positions Snape as the third 'abandoned boy' beside Harry and Voldemort, a half-blood from an unhappy home for whom Hogwarts, as Harry observes, is where all three 'found home.' Voldemort chose power, selfishness, and a fragmented psyche while Harry opened his heart to friends and grew into integrity, and the section asks what makes this 'complicated amalgam of darkness and light,' Dumbledore's double agent and killer, tick.

The section reads Snape's double life through the definition of love shared by writers from Aristotle to Aquinas, willing the good of the other for the other's own sake: he protects people he dislikes because his love for Lily wills their good. As an Occlumens he empties himself of feeling to lie to Voldemort's face, concealing rather than renouncing his love for Lily, and only while dying from Nagini's bite does he freely offer Harry the memories revealing that Harry is a Horcrux.

Tracing Snape's love from the greedy boyhood watching of Lily and the Mudblood rupture through his plea to save Lily alone, which draws Dumbledore's 'You disgust me,' the section judges it short of Aristotle's beloved as a 'second self,' since he wanted Lily's good only as it related to him. Diotima's teaching in the Symposium that 'love is wanting to possess the good forever' and Benedict XVI's love as 'an ongoing exodus out of the closed inward-looking self' frame how Snape's unrequited love gradually 'gives birth in beauty' to virtue in him.

The section argues that vice and virtue are habits built up over time: Snape still rages at Harry-as-James and sneers at Tonks's wolf Patronus as 'weak,' yet his own doe Patronus, matching Lily's, is the magical emblem of his transformation by love. Contrasting friends, who strengthen the soul's integrity by sharing joys and sorrows, with Voldemort, whose Horcruxes give him eight 'selves' while making him less human, it reads remorse as what knits a damaged soul back together, sealed by Harry's forgiveness and the name 'Albus Severus.'

The section collects the love-potion material of Half-Blood Prince: Fred and George's 'violently pink products' at Weasleys' Wizard Wheezes, Amortentia's mother-of-pearl sheen and the smell of freshly mown grass that Hermione dare not finish naming, Slughorn's warning that it causes 'a powerful infatuation or obsession' rather than love, and Ron's Romilda Vane episode from spiked Chocolate Cauldrons. This sets up the chapter's question of what kind of person would actually use one, answered by Voldemort's mother.

chapters.file: ch47 - Real Love or Mere Infatuation.md
chapters.relation: Retelling Dumbledore's reconstruction for Harry, the section sets Merope Gaunt's love potion beside the Imperius Curse, one of the three unforgivable curses that robs victims of their will, as the two ways she might have won Tom Riddle Sr., noting that Harry immediately pairs them as will-robbing magic. Dumbledore's guess that Merope 'could not bear to continue enslaving him' and stopped dosing him, only to be abandoned and left to die, raises the chapter's question of what this loveless origin has to do with the prophecy.

The section argues Merope did not truly love Riddle Sr. because the potion stole his freedom: doing what you want is necessary but not sufficient for freedom, which also requires the ability to do otherwise, the 'libertarian' freedom Tom lacked. It canvasses Harry Frankfurt and the compatibilists who deny that doing-otherwise is necessary yet concedes even they would deny Tom freely loved Merope, and extends the argument to potions taken on oneself, which cheat us of becoming better persons through the hard work of real relationships.

Against the obvious reading of Voldemort's loveless begetting, the section argues he is 'not his mother's son': he imitates Marvolo and Salazar Slytherin, while Merope, on Aristotle's principle that we are what we consistently do, redeemed herself by stopping the potion, renouncing magic entirely, and choosing love over hate at the cost of her life. Character is destiny only if forged by genuinely free choices rather than blood or fate, so Merope shows not even the most tragic beginnings are destined for darkness, while Voldemort, who never loved and never wanted a friend, chose otherwise, leaving Harry as the true mother's son, shielded by 'a more ancient and powerful magic than any potion.'

chapters.file: ch51 - The Feminist Debate So Far.md

chapters.relation: The section maps the feminist critical divide over the series: Schoefer, Heilman, and Gallardo-C. and Smith charge the books with replicating demeaning gender stereotypes, noting no girl is heroic like Harry and no woman wise like Dumbledore, while Kern, Gladstein, and Zettel answer with context, pairing Lavender and Parvati's silliness with Dean and Seamus, Trelawney with fake Lockhart, and Madam Pince with Filch, and pointing to Umbridge and Bellatrix as female villains who command as much fear as any Death Eater. The pervasive giggling girls debate serves as the section's lightning rod.

chapters.file: ch53 - More Wonderful and More Terrible than Death.md
chapters.relation: The section distinguishes liberal feminism, historically grounded in Mary Wollstonecraft, Harriet Taylor Mill, and John Stuart Mill's Enlightenment view that women are rational individuals entitled to equal rights, criticized here for measuring success on masculine terms so that McGonagall and Hermione's achievements count while Molly Weasley's motherhood gets short shrift. It then explains second-wave radical feminism and its 'sex/gender system' analysis of rigid masculine/feminine trait pairings, and reads Gallardo-C. and Smith's 'Cinderfella' interpretation of the series, in which evil displays 'phallic power' even in Umbridge's hypermasculine control while Harry's kindness and selflessness embody feminine values, an association the section traces from St. Gertrude through Gandhi's 'life without love is death' to C.S. Lewis's analysis of the kinds of love.

Reading the series' set pieces as the triumph of traditionally feminine values over masculine aggression, the section moves from Lily's sacrificial love burning Quirrell, through Harry sparing Pettigrew for Lupin's and Sirius's sake, to love expelling Voldemort during the Ministry possession, where 'it was your heart that saved you' and Dumbledore names a force 'more wonderful and more terrible than death.' Harry's kindness to Kreacher, Griphook, and Dobby pays off in the Horcrux hunt, his plea that Voldemort 'try for some remorse' redefines true manhood as incorporating the feminine, and the Forest sacrifice wins the war with a defensive Expelliarmus rather than a duel, showing love more important than aggression.

holes.name: Self-Fulfilling Prophecy
holes.what: A prediction that helps bring about the very event it foretells through the response of those who hear it.
holes.why: Chapter 31 is built around whether Trelawney's prophecy was self-fulfilling through Voldemort's reaction to hearing it, a mechanism that the existing fate-vs-free-will slug (destiny and foreknowledge generally) does not capture.

holes.name: Libertarian Free Will
holes.what: The view that free choices require genuinely open alternatives, the ability to have done otherwise, and so are incompatible with being determined.
holes.why: Chapter 33 defines libertarianism about freedom as the position that makes sense of Rowling's denial of destiny, and the love-potion chapters (48-49) lean on it, but the taxonomy only offers the generic free-will-determinism debate plus compatibilism.
